summary: Provides the network management framework for the MPLS Transport Profile, using ITU-T management terminology. It describes network and element management architectures and ideas for fault, configuration and performance management. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A plan for how people and tools watch over and look after a transport network, from fixing breaks to setting it up.

questions: how should mpls-tp networks be managed
what are the main management functions in mpls-tp
subtitle: How to organize the tools and processes for managing MPLS transport networks

tldr.problem: MPLS-TP is a version of MPLS designed for packet-based transport networks, similar in reliability and management to traditional telecom networks. It needs a management framework that applies established telecommunications principles to managing packet networks.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a network management framework using ITU-T terminology and concepts, describing how network elements, management systems, and operations systems organize into layers. It covers management architectures, fault management, configuration management, and performance management.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now use familiar ITU-T management concepts to operate MPLS-TP networks consistently with existing telecommunications practices.

today: RFC 5950 is an Informational RFC providing the management framework for MPLS-TP. It has not been obsoleted and serves as the basis for MPLS-TP management system design and deployment.

sections.title: Introduction to MPLS-TP Management
sections.content:
MPLS-TP (Multiprotocol Label Switching - Transport Profile) is a version of MPLS designed to provide the capabilities and reliability expected of a packet transport network. Unlike general IP networks, transport networks require strict management, fault detection, and performance monitoring similar to traditional telecommunications systems.

This RFC provides a network management framework for MPLS-TP based on ITU-T management terminology and principles. It builds on the MPLS-TP Requirements document and the MPLS-TP Framework document to explain how network elements and management systems should be organized and how to apply fault management, configuration management, and performance management to MPLS-TP networks.
sections.eli5: A transport network carries important traffic and needs careful management. This explains the organized way to watch over it and keep it running.

sections.title: Network and Element Management Architecture
sections.content:
MPLS-TP networks are managed using a multi-tiered hierarchical architecture. At the lowest tier are the network elements (NEs) that forward traffic and Operations Systems (OSs) that manage them. Each network element contains an Equipment Management Function (EMF) that interacts with management systems and contains management agents, alarms, and configuration logic.

The network management architecture can be partitioned into separate management subnetworks, each serving a geographic region, administrative domain, or load-balanced set of NEs. These subnetworks are connected through management systems. Management communication uses a Data Communication Network (DCN) with separate channels: the Management Communication Channel (MCC) carries management traffic, and the Signaling Communication Channel (SCC) carries control plane signaling.

The EMF of each NE provides FCAPS functions: Fault management for detecting and responding to failures, Configuration management for provisioning services, Accounting management, Performance management for measuring network health, and Security management. These functions interact with the transport functions of the NE via Management Point reference points.
sections.eli5: Each network device has a manager inside it that talks to bigger management systems. The management systems are organized into layers, from local devices up to operations centers, with separate channels for different kinds of messages.

sections.title: Fault Management and Supervision
sections.content:
Fault management provides mechanisms to detect, verify, isolate, notify, and recover from faults. ITU-T G.7710 defines five basic categories of supervision that fulfill these functions. Transmission Supervision detects losses of signal or quality of service, Quality of Service Supervision monitors delay, jitter and loss, Processing Supervision checks computation functions, Hardware Supervision monitors physical equipment, and Environment Supervision monitors temperature, power, and other environmental factors.

The validation process is used to distinguish between fault causes (individual events) and failures (alarms worth reporting). Not every detected event should generate a maintenance alert. The validation process filters events to produce alarms, and the resulting alarms are handled through severity assignment, alarm reporting control, and logging mechanisms. A Management Application Function decides whether to report each event and at what severity level.
sections.eli5: The system watches for problems in five ways: signal loss, quality changes, computing errors, equipment damage, and environmental issues. It learns which problems are real and which are just noise, then tells the right person about the important ones.

sections.title: Configuration Management and LSP Ownership
sections.content:
Configuration management provides the mechanisms to provision MPLS-TP services, set up security, configure and control operations and maintenance (OAM) functions, and manage hardware and software provisioning and inventory. It covers how to create Label Switched Paths (LSPs) that carry traffic through the network.

MPLS-TP networks can be managed by two independent control systems: the Management Plane (using network management systems) and the Control Plane (using signaling protocols). When both are present, each can create and manage LSPs. The entity creating an LSP is its owner and typically controls modifications and deletion. In networks where operators want flexibility, LSP ownership can be transferred from Management Plane to Control Plane after initial setup, allowing manual control of network configuration followed by automatic maintenance. The converse transfer (Control Plane to Management Plane) is less common but useful for maintenance operations.
sections.eli5: Configuration management sets up the paths that traffic follows. Either people or automated systems can create these paths, and they can hand off responsibility from one to the other as needed.

sections.title: Performance Monitoring and Data Control
sections.content:
Performance management collects and analyzes statistics about network health and capacity. These statistics include loss measurements, delay measurements, and throughput metrics. Because performance data can be voluminous, it is important to have flexible instrumentation that controls how much data is collected and reported.

Well-known mechanisms for controlling performance data collection are documented in RFC 2819 (RMON, Remote Monitoring) and RFC 4502 (RMON2). These mechanisms allow filtering and aggregation so that a management network is not overwhelmed by raw statistics. Performance data collection must balance the need for visibility with the need to avoid consuming excess network bandwidth and storage for the management system itself.
sections.eli5: The system measures how well the network is running and how much capacity is available, but it does not send so much information that the measurement itself breaks the network.
